div.b: Two firewall resources, two policies, shared rule groups.
div.span: An endpoint can only live in its own VPC, so ingress and inspection each need their own firewall. Rule groups are shared and versioned in git; the policies differ — ingress blocks inbound exploits and scans, egress does domain allow/deny, TLS inspection and exfil control.

div.b: This whole account is one Terraform module.
div.span:
Written once, then run 30 times with 30 tfvars files. The only value that changes between spokes is the /16, and IPAM hands that out so two spokes can never collide.
A new account is onboarded by Step Functions — that is where automation belongs, not in the packet path.

div.div:
Coming in: user → internet gateway → firewall → load balancer → transit gateway → your app Going out: your app → transit gateway → attachment subnet → firewall → NAT → internet gateway → internet Sideways (east-west): spoke → TGW → inspection VPC → firewall → back to the TGW → the other spoke — it never reaches the NAT gateway
Inside the spoke: application tier → data tier, tcp 5432 / 6379 only — this traffic never leaves the VPC To AWS services: application tier → VPC endpoint — straight to AWS, never crosses a firewall
The coloured arrows are animated and crawl in the direction the packet travels — open the .drawio or the .svg to see it. A .png is a still image and cannot animate.

30 spokes + ingress + inspection + Direct Connect

Network load balancers · 2 ≈ $33/mo + LCU

div.span: 6 services × 2 AZ × 30 spokes = 360 ENIs. This is the line item people miss.

div.b: Rough floor: about $5,000 a month at zero traffic.

div.span: TGW is charged TWICE on east-west — once from the spoke, once on the way back out of inspection.

div.div: Use a GATEWAY endpoint for S3, not an interface one. Gateway endpoints are free. This alone is worth hundreds a month.
Centralise the interface endpoints in shared services and reach them by PrivateLink + Route 53 resolver, instead of 6 per spoke.
Inspect between security zones, not all 30×30. prod↔non-prod and DMZ↔internal, rather than every possible pair.
Re-check whether centralised ingress is required. CloudFront + WAF + an ALB in the spoke removes the ingress VPC, its 2 endpoints and its TGW charges entirely.

div.div: Routes per VPC route table: 50 by default, raisable to 1,000 — but performance degrades above 50. Summarise to 10.0.0.0/8 rather than carrying 30 spoke routes.
Attachments per transit gateway: 5,000 — 33 is nowhere near it.
Route tables per transit gateway: 20 — you use 4.
Routes per TGW route table: 10,000.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 255, 255), rgb(18, 18, 18)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(140, 79, 255), rgb(177, 125, 255));

font-size: 12px; color: light-dark(rgb(68, 81, 95), rgb(158, 170, 182)); margin-top: 6px; line-height: 1.5;
div.div: NAT gateway: 55,000 simultaneous connections to a single destination. A chatty service calling one API endpoint can hit this while total bandwidth looks fine.
NAT gateway: 100 Gbps, scales automatically.
Network Firewall: verify current per-policy rule capacity and throughput against your rule count before committing.
Interface endpoint ENIs count against the VPC ENI quota.

div.b: Hardening and detection still to add

div.style: font-size: 12px; color: light-dark(rgb(68, 81, 95), rgb(158, 170, 182)); margin-top: 6px; line-height: 1.5;
div.div: Route 53 health checks per AZ that run THROUGH the firewall. Without them, a dead firewall endpoint is invisible — see the AZ-failure section below.
Blackhole routes on the TGW for known-bad and unallocated prefixes — standard hardening, currently absent.
Endpoint policies on every VPC endpoint, with an aws:PrincipalOrgID condition. This is the only control on the one uninspected path.
Reachability Analyzer checks wired into CI, so a bad route fails the build rather than production.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 1198px; height: 1px; padding-top: 2616px; margin-left: 13px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #ED7100;
display: inline-block; font-size: 15px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#ED7100, #d86d0c); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; font-weight: bold; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: STILL TO DECIDE — none of these are blocked on code

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 255, 255), rgb(18, 18, 18)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(237, 113, 0), rgb(216, 109, 12));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 914px; height: 1px; padding-top: 2649px; margin-left: 25px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #232F3E;
display: inline-block; font-size: 13px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#232F3E, #bdc7d4); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
font-size: 12px; color: light-dark(rgb(68, 81, 95), rgb(158, 170, 182)); margin-top: 6px; line-height: 1.5;
div.div: Centralised ingress, or distributed? If there is no written requirement that all north-south traffic hits one point, distributed is cheaper and simpler.
Inspect all spoke pairs, or only across zones? Drives the east-west bill directly.
TLS inspection now or later? Needs a private CA and an exclusion list for pinned certificates.
Two AZs or three? Two means losing one costs 50% of capacity; three costs 33%. About +$576/mo in firewall endpoints, plus a NAT.
Is each AZ sized to carry the FULL load? This, not the diagram, is what decides whether HA actually works.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 255, 255), rgb(18, 18, 18)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(237, 113, 0), rgb(216, 109, 12));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 914px; height: 1px; padding-top: 2649px; margin-left: 985px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #232F3E;
display: inline-block; font-size: 13px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#232F3E, #bdc7d4); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
font-size: 12px; color: light-dark(rgb(68, 81, 95), rgb(158, 170, 182)); margin-top: 6px; line-height: 1.5;
div.div: Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN? TGW is right for 30 accounts in one region. If a second region is genuinely coming, Cloud WAN's policy-based segmentation is where new builds are going — decide before you build, not after.
AWS Network Firewall or third-party via GWLB? Both are standard. Third-party wins when you already own the licences and the operational muscle.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 255, 255), rgb(18, 18, 18)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(237, 113, 0), rgb(216, 109, 12));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 914px; height: 1px; padding-top: 2649px; margin-left: 1945px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #232F3E;
display: inline-block; font-size: 13px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#232F3E, #bdc7d4); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
font-size: 12px; color: light-dark(rgb(68, 81, 95), rgb(158, 170, 182)); margin-top: 6px; line-height: 1.5;
div.div: The diagram says "peering: region 2". That is a note, not a design.
Decide the posture: pilot light, warm standby, or active-active. Each implies a different second-region hub, a different RTO, and a very different bill.
Until that is decided, a region-wide failure has no answer. Zonal shift covers one AZ, not a region.

div.div: FIRST, THE THING PEOPLE GET WRONG

div.b: An AZ is not one datacentre

div.style: font-size: 12px; color: light-dark(rgb(68, 81, 95), rgb(158, 170, 182)); margin-top: 6px; line-height: 1.5;
div.div:
Region — e.g. ap-south-1
↳ Availability Zone — one or more datacentres
↳ datacentre · own power, cooling, network
↳ datacentre
Losing one datacentre usually does not take the AZ down — AWS absorbs it inside the AZ.
A full AZ loss is the bigger and much rarer event. That is what the rest of this page assumes.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 255, 255), rgb(18, 18, 18)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(1, 168, 141), rgb(14, 157, 134));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 914px; height: 1px; padding-top: 3031px; margin-left: 985px;

font-size: 12px; color: light-dark(rgb(68, 81, 95), rgb(158, 170, 182)); margin-top: 6px; line-height: 1.5;
div.div:
user → Route 53 → CloudFront + WAF → IGW
→ firewall endpoint AZ-b ✓ (AZ-a ✗)
→ NLB node AZ-b → TGW
→ spoke ALB AZ-b → EC2 AZ-b
The NLB has one IP per AZ. AZ-a's IP leaves DNS, so new connections can only land in AZ-b.
Cross-zone OFF is what keeps it clean — AZ-b's node only ever serves AZ-b targets.

font-size: 12px; color: light-dark(rgb(68, 81, 95), rgb(158, 170, 182)); margin-top: 6px; line-height: 1.5;
div.div:
EC2 AZ-b → spoke route table AZ-b → TGW ENI AZ-b
→ TGW · appliance mode keeps it in AZ-b
→ attachment subnet 10.100.0.16/28
→ firewall endpoint AZ-b → NAT AZ-b → IGW → internet
AZ-a's NAT, firewall endpoint and ENI simply sit unused.
Nothing fails over. No route is rewritten. No Lambda runs. The AZ-b path was already live and carrying traffic, which is how you know it works.

div.div: WHAT IS CAUGHT AUTOMATICALLY — AND WHAT IS NOT

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 255, 255), rgb(18, 18, 18)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 161, 22), rgb(97, 130, 11));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 914px; height: 1px; padding-top: 3273px; margin-left: 25px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #232F3E;
display: inline-block; font-size: 13px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#232F3E, #bdc7d4); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
font-size: 12px; color: light-dark(rgb(68, 81, 95), rgb(158, 170, 182)); margin-top: 6px; line-height: 1.5;
div.div: All targets in AZ-a unhealthy → the NLB pulls AZ-a's IP out of DNS. No configuration needed beyond having health checks.
Whole AZ impaired and AWS detects it → ARC zonal autoshift moves traffic out — but only if autoshift is enabled. Plain zonal shift is a manual action.
RDS Multi-AZ promotes the AZ-b standby on its own.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 255, 255), rgb(18, 18, 18)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(221, 52, 76), rgb(255, 127, 147));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 914px; height: 1px; padding-top: 3273px; margin-left: 985px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #232F3E;
display: inline-block; font-size: 13px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#232F3E, #bdc7d4); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
font-size: 12px; color: light-dark(rgb(68, 81, 95), rgb(158, 170, 182)); margin-top: 6px; line-height: 1.5;

div.b: The firewall endpoint in AZ-a dies while the targets stay healthy.

div.div: The firewall sits before the NLB: IGW → firewall → NLB. But the NLB health-checks the other way: NLB → TGW → spoke ALB → EC2. That path never touches firewall 1.
So the NLB sees green, keeps advertising AZ-a's IP, and traffic arriving there is blackholed at the dead endpoint.

div.b: Fix: Route 53 health checks, one per AZ, that traverse the firewall end to end.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 255, 255), rgb(18, 18, 18)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(140, 79, 255), rgb(177, 125, 255));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 914px; height: 1px; padding-top: 3273px; margin-left: 1945px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #232F3E;
display: inline-block; font-size: 13px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#232F3E, #bdc7d4); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
font-size: 12px; color: light-dark(rgb(68, 81, 95), rgb(158, 170, 182)); margin-top: 6px; line-height: 1.5;
div.div: NLB DNS TTL is 60 seconds — clients may hold the old IP that long.
Some clients cache DNS forever on default settings (Java, notably). Set networkaddress.cache.ttl or they will keep hitting the dead AZ.
RDS Multi-AZ promotion: typically 60–120 seconds.
Connections already open through AZ-a are dropped instantly and recovered by client retry.

div.b: Realistic recovery is one to two minutes, not instant. Retry logic in the client is mandatory.

div.div: WHAT YOU STILL HAVE TO TURN ON OR DECIDE

div.div: Route 53 health check per AZ, through the firewall path — closes the gap above.
CloudWatch alarm on Network Firewall endpoint status.
CloudWatch alarm on a sudden rise in DroppedPackets.
CloudWatch alarm on TGW blackhole packet count.
Enable ARC zonal autoshift, not just zonal shift.
Drop an AZ with FIS at least once a year and watch all of the above fire.

div.b: Every box in the architecture above can say HA and the site can still go down.

div.div: Each AZ at 50% utilisation → losing one costs nothing.
Each AZ at 90% utilisation → losing one takes you down.
Decide: is each AZ sized to carry the full load (N+1)?
Two AZs = lose 50%. Three AZs = lose 33%, for roughly +$576/mo in firewall endpoints plus a NAT.
A single Direct Connect is a single point of failure. Two connections at two DX locations, or accept VPN-speed fallback.

display: inline-block; font-size: 13px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#232F3E, #bdc7d4); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.b: The failure zonal shift cannot fix

div.style: font-size: 12px; color: light-dark(rgb(68, 81, 95), rgb(158, 170, 182)); margin-top: 6px; line-height: 1.5;
div.div: A bad rule push. Both firewalls share rule groups, so a rule that drops everything hits both AZs at once. That is not an AZ failure — there is no healthy AZ to shift to.
Deploy rule changes in ALERT mode first, watch the drop rate, then flip to drop.
Stage through a non-prod firewall running the same policy.
Rule groups versioned in git, with a rollback you have actually tested.

div.b: Honestly: a bad rule is a far likelier outage than an AZ losing its firewall endpoint.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 2858px; height: 1px; padding-top: 3803px; margin-left: 13px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #5C6875;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#5C6875, #8d97a2); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div: The original design put a standby firewall in AZ-2 and a Lambda to fail over to it. That is strictly worse: the standby is idle, so you only find out whether it works during an outage, and the failover itself becomes a new way to fail. Here both paths carry traffic every second, so both are proven continuously, and an AZ loss needs no action at all.
